title: Gargi's Two Arrows
hook: at a king's great debate, one questioner wants to find out and another wants to win; Nyaya names the difference
carry: vada: talk that seeks the truth, not the win
tomorrow: a golden deer, and a cry in Rama's voice. why did Sita believe it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nyaya's argument in five parts, said out loud, with the example doing the real work: where's your pot? A new week begins.

King Janaka has called the wisest people in the land to his sacrifice, and he's set out a prize: a thousand cows, with gold tied to their horns. They go, he says, to the one who knows Brahman best. A sage named Yajnavalkya doesn't wait. He tells his student: drive them home. The hall erupts. One by one, the learned stand up to question him. Two of them matter today. A woman named Gargi, who wants to know. And a man named Shakalya, who wants Yajnavalkya to lose. Same hall, same questions flying. Very different talk.
screen: `A THOUSAND COWS, GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.` → `GARGI WANTS TO KNOW.` → `SHAKALYA WANTS TO WIN.`

segments.voice: This is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. Gargi goes first. On what is water woven, she asks, like thread on a loom? On air. And air? She climbs, world by world, until Yajnavalkya stops her: Gargi, don't question too far. She sits down. But she comes back. Like a warrior stringing a bow with two arrows, she says, I have two questions. What is everything woven on, past, present and future? Space. And space? The imperishable, the seer no one sees. Then Gargi turns to the hall and says: none of you will beat him. She came to find out, and when she found out, she said so. Then Shakalya. He pushes and pushes, and Yajnavalkya asks him: have these scholars made you their tongs, to pull hot coals out of the fire for them? The text says it ended badly for him. Centuries later, the Nyaya Sutra named what happens in a hall like that. Vada is discussion where both sides reason honestly to find out, the kind you have with teachers, students and fellow seekers who aren't jealous. Jalpa is wrangling to win, with tricks. Vitanda is only knocking down, with no view of your own. Reading Gargi as vada and Shakalya as jalpa is our reading; the Sutra came later. But this is why Hindu learning treats debate, shastrartha, as a way to seek the truth, and why the Sutra allows hard wrangling only as a thorny fence around a young seed of truth. So at any table today, the question is: am I Gargi, or Shakalya?
screen: `VADA: TALK THAT WANTS TO FIND OUT.` · `JALPA: TALK THAT WANTS TO WIN.` · `VITANDA: ONLY KNOCKING DOWN.` · `GARGI, OR SHAKALYA?` · then, large: `FIND OUT, OR WIN?`

segments.voice: Before your next hard conversation, at home, at work or online, try what teachers and students chant before study: om saha navavatu, ending ma vidvishavahai, may we not turn against each other. If you don't pray, say its meaning in your own words. Then sit with the breath and replay one recent disagreement, without rearguing it. Were you asking, like Gargi, or aiming, like Shakalya?
Nyaya. Today, its three kinds of talk: vada, honest discussion that seeks the truth; jalpa, wrangling to win; and vitanda, only knocking down.
Your line: vada, talk that seeks the truth, not the win. Gargi asked, listened, and said so. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit schools, students learn Nyaya through vada with a teacher and through formal debate, shastrartha; teacher and students often chant 'om saha navavatu' before study, asking that they not turn against each other.

fork.setup: at a family dinner, your uncle and cousin are arguing politics, and you have a strong view. by the Nyaya Sutra and Gargi's example, what's vada here?
options: ask one real question, and be ready to say 'you've got a point'.
stay quiet: Hindu tradition says never to argue.
find the weakest thing they said and hammer it till they give up.
fork.reveal: vada is honest talk aimed at the truth. Gargi pressed hard, then said plainly when she'd been answered. hammering to win is jalpa.

original.note: Sanskrit: vada, discussion; in Nyaya, honest talk aimed at the truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: an argument is an argument.
what it means: Hindu learning treats honest debate as a way to seek the truth. Nyaya calls it vada, and tells it apart from wrangling to win and attacking with no view of your own.
